metaDescription: Five long-reach drywall sanders under $300 with vacuum ports, compared on motor type, head design, speed range and how much dust actually gets captured.
expertTake: The WEN DW5084 is the pick for most remodelers, because a dual-head design with triangular and circular pads, a 15 foot dust hose and a head-mounted 5 amp motor gives it real reach without a gimmick. The KUPERIA is the choice if you want the strongest stated motor and a detachable corner edge. Skip a powered drywall sander if you only patch a few screw holes, because a hand pole sander with a vacuum adapter is cheaper and gives you more control on small repairs.
introParagraphs: A powered drywall sander is a long pole with a rotating head and a vacuum path, built to smooth joint compound across walls and ceilings without a ladder or a cloud of white dust. The numbers on the box tell you about the motor, but whether the sander leaves a flat joint or a dished one depends on head design and how you control it.

This guide explains what a spending cap of $300 buys, what you give up against a pro dust-free system, and which specs predict a smooth wall. Our top picks are above, with full reviews below. Prices move, and the cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: WEN DW5084 5 Amp 2-in-1 Dual-Head Drywall Sander with 15 ft Hose
products.description:
The WEN DW5084 mounts a 5 amp motor right at the head, which means the torque reaches the disc without a long drive shaft that robs power. A head-mounted motor is heavier at the end of the pole than a rear-mounted design, but it pushes more force into the abrasive and keeps the head spinning under pressure. Variable speed from 600 to 1500 RPM lets you slow down for finishing and speed up for ridges.

The 2-in-1 design is its distinguishing feature: a triangular pad for corners and a circular pad for flat areas, both attached with hook and loop and swapped without tools. A triangle reaches the angle where a wall meets a ceiling, which a round disc cannot do. A 15 foot hose connects to a shop vacuum and gives you reach across a room.

The tradeoff against the VEVOR and MAXXT is that the vacuum is separate, so you need your own shop vacuum with good filtration. Check that the hose adapter fits your vacuum, and use fine discs, 120 to 220 grit, to avoid gouging. A good technique is to sand at a shallow angle with a work light held beside the wall, since raking light shows ridges that overhead lighting hides. Prime before judging the final result, because paint shows every imperfection the bare compound hides.
products.bestFor: Remodelers who sand corners and flat walls and already own a shop vacuum.
pros: Triangular and circular heads swap without tools
Head-mounted 5 amp motor delivers strong torque at the disc
Variable speed from 600 to 1500 RPM suits rough and fine work
15 foot hose gives reach across a room
cons: Needs a separate shop vacuum with good filtration
Head-mounted motor adds weight at the end of the pole
Hose adapters may not fit every vacuum

products.name: KUPERIA 8.5 Amp Drywall Sander with Built-In Vacuum, LED and Corner Edge
products.description:
KUPERIA quotes the strongest motor in the roundup, 8.5 amps of copper winding, with seven speeds from 800 to 1800 RPM and a built-in vacuum. Built-in means the fan sits inside the sander, so it pulls dust through a dual pipe channel without needing a separate shop vacuum. That convenience matters for homeowners who do not own a heavy vacuum.

An LED light shines across the work, which lets you see ridges and low spots in raking light, and a detachable corner edge lets you reach into the angle where wall meets ceiling. The tradeoff is that built-in vacuums capture less dust than a connected shop vacuum, so wear a respirator regardless. Against the WEN, the KUPERIA has more motor and a built-in fan, but only one head shape in the box.

Watch the head weight on overhead work, and let the tool do the work instead of pressing. Replace the pad when the hooks wear, and empty the dust container often. On a long ceiling, rest the pole against your shoulder to carry some weight, and take breaks, since a heavy head tires the arms fast. Remember that the LED helps spot ridges but does not replace a proper work light.
products.bestFor: Homeowners without a shop vacuum who want a self-contained sander.
pros: 8.5 amp motor is the strongest claim in this roundup
Built-in vacuum means no separate shop vacuum required
LED light shows ridges and low spots in raking light
Detachable corner edge reaches wall and ceiling angles
cons: Built-in vacuum captures less dust than a shop vacuum
Pole-mounted fan and motor add weight overhead
Lesser known brand with limited parts support

products.name: MAXXT 810W Handheld Drywall Sander, 1500-2800 RPM
products.description:
MAXXT takes a different approach with an 810 watt motor and a speed range of 1500 to 2800 RPM, the fastest in the group. A fast head cuts joint compound quickly, which is useful for rough sanding of flat walls, while the slower end of the range handles fine finishing. Two modes, rough and fine, are the maker's framing for the same variable speed.

The design keeps dust out of the motor, which extends its life, since drywall dust is fine enough to clog a motor's windings. A larger light switch is easier to press and less prone to accidental operation. The tradeoff is that high speed leaves deeper scratches if you linger, and it can gouge soft compound. Against the WEN, the MAXXT spins much faster, so it needs more care.

Start with 120 grit and keep the sander moving in overlapping passes. Use a work light across the wall to check for ridges before you prime. If you take it to a textured wall, remember that high speed also removes texture quickly, so test on a hidden patch first. Keep a spare set of discs nearby, as high speed wears them quickly.
products.bestFor: Quick, flat walls where speed matters and you keep the head moving.
pros: 1500 to 2800 RPM is the fastest range in this roundup
Dust-sealed motor extends service life
Large light switch is easier to operate with gloves
Works for both rough and fine sanding
cons: High speed can gouge soft joint compound if you linger
Few published details on the dust system
Little brand support if a part fails

products.name: VEVOR 800W Drywall Sander with 12 Discs and Vacuum System
products.description:
VEVOR ships the most accessories, with 12 sanding discs, an 800 watt brush motor and a variable speed of 1200 to 2300 RPM. A brush motor is the standard, inexpensive design that can be serviced by replacing brushes, and 800 watts is comparable to the 8.5 amp KUPERIA at standard voltage.

The vacuum is built in and removes dust automatically, which the maker pitches as less dust and more visibility. The tradeoff is the same as with the KUPERIA: an onboard vacuum cannot match a shop vacuum for capture, and it adds weight to the pole. Against the MAXXT, the VEVOR's speed range is lower but the disc supply is much bigger.

Use the 12 discs to start with 120 and move to 180, saving the finest for final passes. Check the brushes after a few jobs and keep the vents clear of dust. With 12 discs in the box, one set of coarse, medium and fine grits covers an average room without a second purchase. Keep the discs flat in a zip bag so they do not curl before you use them.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want discs and a built-in vacuum in one box.
pros: 12 sanding discs included, enough for a whole room
Built-in vacuum removes dust without a shop vacuum
1200 to 2300 RPM variable speed suits rough and fine work
800 W brush motor can be serviced with new brushes
cons: Onboard vacuum captures less dust than a shop vacuum
Heavier at the end of the pole than a plain sander
Brush motors wear faster than brushless designs

products.name: IMQUALI 8-Amp Collapsible Drywall Sander with Built-In Vacuum
products.description:
IMQUALI's sander collapses so it fits into a carry bag, which is a practical benefit if you work from a car or a small closet. An 8 amp copper motor drives a disc with a 10-hole pattern, and a built-in vacuum pulls dust through those holes. More holes means a more even suction across the disc, which reduces the dust ring around the edge.

The tool is also marketed for popcorn ceiling removal, which is a job where dust capture matters, since old ceiling texture can contain materials you should not breathe. The tradeoff is the same as other built-in vacuums: capture is partial, and a respirator is still required. Against the KUPERIA, the IMQUALI has a slightly smaller motor but a collapsible pole.

Wear a respirator rated for fine dust, especially on older ceilings. Empty the container often, and replace discs as they clog. Because the pole collapses, the sander also suits a basement or a crawlspace where a rigid pole would not fit. Lightweight carry bags also protect the head from damage on the truck.
products.bestFor: Small jobs and ceiling work where storage and portability matter.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A round disc smooths flat walls, and a triangular pad reaches the angle where a wall meets a ceiling. The WEN DW5084 ships both heads, and the KUPERIA has a detachable corner edge. Without a corner solution, you will still be hand-sanding every inside corner. Inside corners are where hand sanding takes the most time, so a corner solution saves hours on a whole room.

A built-in fan is convenient but captures only part of the dust, while a connected shop vacuum captures much more. The WEN DW5084 relies on your shop vacuum through a 15 foot hose, and the KUPERIA, VEVOR and IMQUALI have built-in systems. Fine drywall dust is a health hazard, so wear a respirator either way. Pair either style with a plastic sheet over the doorway and a box fan blowing outward, which keeps dust from spreading through the house.

A stronger motor holds speed under pressure, and a wider range gives control. The KUPERIA's 8.5 amps and the IMQUALI's 8 amps lead on motor claims, and the MAXXT's 1500 to 2800 RPM leads on speed. Too much speed gouges soft compound, so slow down for finishing. A motor that is strong but unbalanced still leaves wavy joints, so technique matters as much as power.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Weight and balance on the pole
buyingCriteria.explanation: Overhead sanding is tiring, and a heavy head at the end of the pole makes it worse. A head-mounted motor like the WEN's adds weight at the tip, and built-in fans add more. Check the total weight and the pole length before you buy. Many buyers underestimate pole length: an 8 foot ceiling needs a pole that reaches without strain.

Hook and loop discs change in seconds, and a good supply saves trips to the store. The VEVOR ships 12 discs and the KUPERIA six, while the WEN needs separate discs. A 10-hole pattern like the IMQUALI's must match the disc. A pack of mixed grits is also useful when you move from rough joint compound to a skim coat.

A powered sander speeds up large areas, but a hand sander gives more control on small repairs. For a few screw holes, a vacuum hand sander is cheaper and safer. Powered sanders reward big rooms and whole-wall finishing. A powered sander also removes material quickly, so a heavy hand can sand through the tape on a joint.

specDecoder.meaning: Rotations per minute of the sanding head. Higher RPM cuts faster but gouges softer compound, and it also throws more dust into the air.
specDecoder.watchFor: The MAXXT's 2800 RPM top speed is much higher than the WEN's 1500.

specDecoder.meaning: Current draw and power input. A bigger motor holds speed under pressure.
specDecoder.watchFor: VEVOR's 800 W and MAXXT's 810 W are about 6.7 amps, below the KUPERIA's 8.5.

specDecoder.meaning: A motor placed at the sanding head, giving direct torque without a drive shaft. It trades extra weight at the pole tip for more power at the disc.
specDecoder.watchFor: It adds weight at the end of the pole, which is tiring overhead.

specDecoder.meaning: The holes in the disc that pull dust into the vacuum. More holes spread suction.
specDecoder.watchFor: The IMQUALI's 10-hole disc needs matching replacements.

specDecoder.meaning: The size of abrasive particles. Drywall sanding typically uses 120 to 220 grit, and a finer grit gives a smoother surface under paint.
specDecoder.watchFor: Coarse grit under 100 leaves scratches that show through paint.

howWeEvaluated.title: Head design
howWeEvaluated.description: We began with how each sander reaches corners. The WEN's dual heads and the KUPERIA's corner edge led. We treated a corner solution as essential, since inside angles consume most of the hand-sanding time on a room.

howWeEvaluated.title: Dust control
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared built-in and connected vacuums. The WEN's 15 foot hose and the IMQUALI's 10-hole disc stood out. We also considered whether the dust path could connect to a shop vacuum.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at motor claims and speed range. The KUPERIA at 8.5 amps and MAXXT at 2800 RPM led.

howWeEvaluated.title: Included supplies
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered discs and accessories. The VEVOR's 12 discs and the IMQUALI's carry bag stood out.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted recurring themes such as head weight and dust leakage. Lesser known labels were scored cautiously for parts support.

maintenance.why: Clogged discs burn compound and scratch the wall, and they overheat the motor. Fresh discs cut cooler, so swap them before they glaze.

maintenance.task: Empty the dust container or filter
maintenance.why: A full container blocks airflow. Empty it often.
Drywall dust is fine enough to clog motor vents and shorten the motor's life. Blow them out with compressed air after each job, outdoors if possible.
Leaks lower suction. Replace damaged hoses.
Worn brushes cause weak power. Replace them in pairs.

faq.q: Do I need a powered drywall sander?
faq.a: For large areas, yes, since it saves time and effort. For a few repairs, a hand sander is enough, and it gives better control around fixtures.

faq.q: What does $300 buy in a drywall sander?
faq.a: A long-reach sander with a 5 to 8.5 amp motor and a vacuum port or fan. You give up pro-grade dust extraction. The cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated.
Use 120 to 220 grit, and avoid coarse grit that leaves scratches.
It helps, but wear a respirator anyway. A shop vacuum captures more dust, so use one if you can and seal the room with plastic sheeting.

faq.q: Can I use it to remove popcorn ceiling?
faq.a: Some can, but old ceilings may contain hazardous materials, so test before you sand. If the texture is old, a professional abatement may be the safer path.
Yes. Drywall dust is fine and harmful to breathe, so wear a respirator rated for fine dust, plus eye protection. Run a box fan to the outdoors in the work room.
